messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: secr.test and overdispersion
parts:
Good day group members,

We expect overdispersion in our data because animals are sometimes detected in groups.  Does the output from secr.test with fit = TRUE (deviance / residual df ) constitute (or allow one to calculate) an estimate of the variance inflation factor?

Thanks,
Eric

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: secr.test and overdispersion
parts:
To be clear, and to encourage others to reply: secr.test is just a way to simulate data under the model, re-fit the model, and collect some statistic(s) (default deviance/df). You could use the ratio of observed to simulated deviance/df to estimate a c-hat-like variance inflation factor, but that will combine  all sorts of model mis-specification and overdispersion, not just grouping of individuals. It's not guaranteed to be a good estimate. To my knowledge no-one has yet addressed overdispersion in SECR models - do you have (a lot of) time on your hands? :-)
Murray

messages.subject: Re: secr.test and overdispersion
parts:
Hi,

Thanks for responding, Murray.  I might be able to devote some time to this problem.  In camera-trapping surveys of primates, multiple individuals are frequently detected in a single photo or video.   I'm also aware that lack of model structure can contribute to overdispersion and that it could be difficult to separate sources of overdispersion in real data. We could probably simulate data where overdispersion results only from grouping of individuals, and otherwise the data conform to the specified model(?).
Eric

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: secr.test and overdispersion
parts:
Good that you may be able to look at overdispersion - certainly crops up with social species (wolves etc.). Your particular problem (group photos) sounds to me like one that could be tackled directly rather than via this indirect route. Note the clone() function in 'secr'. This generates overdispersion with constant, Poisson or binomial number per cluster; there is a default method and one for 'popn' objects (I was interested in multiple sounds from a point), but not currently one to replicate rows of capthist objects. I'll fix that when I get a chance.
Murray

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: secr.test and overdispersion
parts:
Many thanks for your previous responses, and for adding this clone method, Murray.
I am going to try some simulations with overdispersed data.
I tried to first confirm that chat, calculated as observed dev/df : (mean of) simulated dev/df, is generally close to 1.0 when there is no overdispersion and the model is specified correctly. I used the code below, and variations of it with e.g. more traps, variable and more complex trap layouts, and higher lambda0, to estimate chat. I seem consistently get estimates of chat close to 1.14 or 1.15 (see example histogram below code). 

Before I accept this result, I want to be sure that the tendency for chat to be >1 isn't due to model mis-specification caused by my code. As far as I can tell, the data generated and the model fitted 99 times by secr.test() should match the original ("observed") objects ch and fit1. Can anyone see any reason why it wouldn't?

I realize I should probably increase both the number of iterations and the nsim argument to e.g. 500 or 1000, but can't see why failing to do so at this early stage would induce systematic bias.

Thanks in advance,
Eric


gr = make.grid(nx=8, ny=8, spacing = 100,detector="count", originxy=c(500,500))
cr = make.grid(nx=2, ny=2, spacing = 1800) # core for sim.popn
mesh = make.mask(gr, buffer=400, spacing=100, type="trapbuffer")
#
# function to extract statistics during sims (for use with secr.test())  
#
extfn = function(object) {
  c(dev=deviance(object), df=df.residual(object), devdf=deviance(object) / df.residual(object),
   Dhat = exp(coefficients(object)[1,1]))
}
#
# empty vector for chat values; start loop across iterations
#
chat = vector()
#
for (i in 1:100) {
  print(i)
  pp = sim.popn(0.5, cr, 0)
  ch = sim.capthist(gr, pp, detectfn=14, detectpar=list(lambda0=1,sigma=100),noccasions=1)
  fit1 = secr.fit(ch, model=list(lambda0~1,sigma~1), mask=mesh, detectfn=14, start=list(lambda0=1,sigma=100),trace=F)
  gf = secr.test(fit1, nsim=99, statfn=extfn, fit=T)
  obstosim =  gf$output$observed[3] / mean(gf$output$simulated[3,])
  chat[i] = obstosim
}
#
summary(chat)
hist(chat)
#

Good day,
After using the clone() method on a capthist object to generate overdispersed data, the resulting capthist object had different dimensions (the number of occasions (1) was dropped).
This was easy to fix in this case, but only because the number of replicate encounter histories was held constant in the call to clone().
I'm using secr version 2.10.3.


> pp = sim.popn(0.1, cr, 0)
> ch.g = sim.capthist(gr, pp, detectfn=14, detectpar=list(lambda0=1,sigma=100),noccasions=1)
> ch = clone(ch.g, "constant", 6)

[1]  7  1 64

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: secr.test and overdispersion
parts:
Damn. The old 'dropped dimension' bug. As Spencer Graves says in The R Inferno

"NOTE: Failing to use drop=FALSE inside functions is a major source of bugs.
You only test the function when the subscript has length greater than 1. The
function fails once it hits a situation where the subscript is length 1|somewhere
downstream a matrix is expected and there is a simple vector there instead."

I'll try to get a fixed version out ASAP.

I'm not seeing problems with your other code. I never knew that coefficients would work as an alias for coef in secr, but I see that it does! A hint - you probably want to design your simulations to use multiple cores.

Murray

I think this is now fixed in the interim version of 2.10.4 on the Density website http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/. I hope to publish that to CRAN in the next week or so. This works for me:

library(secr) # 2.10.4 from 2016-11-29
gr <- make.grid(nx=10, ny=10, detector='proximity')
cr <- gr
for (i in 1:5) {
    pp = sim.popn(0.2, cr, 0)

ch.g = sim.capthist(gr, pp, detectfn=14, detectpar=list(lambda0=1,sigma=100),noccasions=1)
    ch = clone(ch.g, "constant", 6)

cat ("\n i = ",i, "\n")
    print(dim(ch.g))
    print(dim(ch))
    print(summary(ch))
}
